HEARD:  March 7
& 8, 2006

(at
Hamilton
)

LOFCHIK J.

[
1
]

The Children’s Aid
Society of Hamilton is bringing a motion for summary judgment for a final order
to be made, without trial, seeking a finding that the children are in need of protection
pursuant to s. 37(2)(b)(i); 37(2)(f)and 37(2)(g) of the
Child and Family Services Act
, and making the children wards of the
Society for a period of six months, with access to the mother and father at the
discretion of the Society and supervised at the discretion of the Society.

[
2
]

The children have been
placed with their older sibling, N.H., since November 12, 2004. N.H. has been
approved as an interim kinship foster placement for the children and the
children remain in that placement to date.

[
3
]

The Society has been
working with the parents for approximately two years. Throughout this
involvement, the Society alleges that the parents have been unco-operative and
have failed to follow through with the Society’s request to address protection
concerns, which include serious domestic violence and mental health issues.

[
4
]

The subject children are M.R.H.,
born […], 1991, currently 14 years old; L.H., born […], 1995, currently 10
years old; and S.H., born […], 1997, currently eight years old. On
May 18, 2005

a temporary Order was granted by LaFreniere J. placing the children in the care
of the Society. The children are currently placed in the kinship care of their
sibling, N.H., who has been approved as a foster placement for the children.

[
5
]

The parents’ access to the
children is currently supervised at the Society’s office for one hour, once per
week. The mother has not attended access visits since October 2005.

[
6
]

On November 12, 2004, the
mother voluntarily placed the children in the care of their adult sibling, N.H.,
born […], 1984, currently 21 years old. The children have remained in N.H. care
since this date. In May, 2005, N.H. and her husband, D.W. were approved as an
interim kinship foster placement.

[
7
]

The mother of the
children is W.H., born […], 1965, currently 41 years old. She is currently
residing in
Newmarket
and is separated from the father.

[
8
]

The father of the
children is J.H.. The mother and father resided together at the time of the
children’s birth and the Society concedes that he qualifies as a parent within
the meaning of the
Act
.

[
9
]

On
May 13, 2005
,
the children were apprehended from the care of their older sibling, N.H., and
placed in the care of the Society, with N.H. and her husband, D.W., as a
kinship foster placement. A protection application was commenced because N.H.
had requested additional support from the Society in order to care for the
children, which could be achieved by approving her home as a kinship foster
placement and because there continue to be numerous unaddressed protection
concerns with respect to the parents.

[
10
]

The concerns that existed
with respect to the parents at the time of the apprehension included the
family’s longstanding involvement with the Society; the parents’ history of
domestic violence, which the children had witnessed and have disclosed made
them afraid; the fact that the mother had charges against the father for
assault on at least two occasions; and the father had a history of severe
mental health issues and had received treatment.

[
11
]

The mother agreed at the
time of the apprehension that she was not in a position to care for the
children.

[
12
]

On May 18, 2005, the
Society commenced a protection application seeking a finding that the children
were in need of protection pursuant to s. 37(2)(b)(i); 37(2)(f); and 37(2)(g)
of the
Child and Family
Services Act
. The
Society sought an order making the children wards of the Society for a period
of six months with access to the parents in the discretion of the Society and
supervised in the discretion of the Society.

[
13
]

As the parents were unrepresented,
Czutrin J., made an order on January 23, 2006 that each parent could give reply
evidence in the summary judgment motion,
viva voce
at the hearing and
this has taken place.

LAW

[
14
]

The summary judgment
process is available in child protection matters under the provisions of the
Family Law Rules
(see Rule 16(2) of the
Family Law Rules
).

[
15
]

The test is whether there
is a genuine issue requiring a trial of a claim or defence. (Ref: Rule 16(6) of
the
Family Law Rules
)

[
16
]

Unlike its civil
counterpart, Rule 20, Rule 16 of the
Family Law Rules
,
contains no subrule providing that a responding party may not rest upon a
denial in a pleading but must also file an affidavit or other evidence setting
out specific facts showing that there is a genuine issue for trial. Nevertheless,
common sense dictates that a respondent who files no evidence runs an enhanced
risk of suffering judgment based upon the moving party’s evidence. (Ref.
R.A. v. Jewish Family & Child Service

[2001] O.J. No. 47
at para. 11
)

[
17
]

Although Rule 16 does not
expressly require a party to set out in affidavit form those facts which show
the genuine issue for trial, the parents must do more than deny some material
fact. A party cannot rest on a denial and he must put his best foot forward.
Otherwise the rule might as well be repealed. (Ref.
Bruvels v. Guindon

2000 CanLII 28163 (ON SC)
,
[2000] O.J. No. 875 (SCJ)
;
R.A. v. Jewish Family and Child Service

[2001] O.J. No. 47
at para. 21
)

[
18
]

In interpreting Rule 16,
Rule 2 of the
Family Court
Rules
must also be
considered. Also, subsection 1(1) of the
Child and Family Services Act
providing that the paramount purpose of the
Act
is to promote the best interests, protection and well-being of
children is necessary to the interpretation of the
Rules
. (Ref. Rule 2 of the
Family Law Rules
;
ss 1(1) of the
Child and
Family Services Act
;
Children’s Aid Society of Hamilton v. M.W.

2003 CanLII 2309 (ON SC)
,
[2003] O.J. No. 220
at paras.
24 and 25
)

[
19
]

It is no longer necessary
that every case be
“the clearest of cases”
. Rule 16 does not so provide
and, given the procedures in place to make such rules, the omission cannot be
unintentional. Caution is called for, but if the evidence does not raise a
triable issue as to where the best interests of the children lie, those best
interests themselves call for a resolution without the delay associated with a
trial and the resulting prolongation of the state of uncertainty about the
child’s future. (Ref.
R.A.
v. Jewish Family and Child Service
,

supra
, at para. 20)

[
20
]

The factors to be
considered in determining the best interests of a child are contained in s. 37
of the
Child and Family
Services Act
.

[
21
]

In child protection
proceedings, the genuiness of an issue must arise from something more than a
heartfelt expression of a parent’s desire to resume care of the child. There
must be an arguable notion discernible from the parents’ evidence that they
face some better prospect than what existed at the time of the Society’s
removal of the child from their care and have developed some new ability as
parents. (Ref.
C.A.S. of
Toronto v. R.H.

2000 CanLII 3158 (ON CJ)
,
[2000]
O.J. No. 5853
at paras.
17
, 18, 28 and 32)

[
22
]

The court must assume
that a responding parent has
“put their best foot forward”
in the
responding material and that this is the most they have to offer at this stage.

“The questions becomes, how long is it reasonable to leave the children on
hold and in limbo while it is determined whether another attempt to change the
behaviour of the parents will succeed?”
(Ref.
Kawartha-Haliburton C.A.S. v. W.M.
(2003)
2003 CanLII 2441 (ON SC)
,
O.J. No. 3903
at paras.
60 and 61
)

ANALYSIS

[
23
]

The evidence which the
Society has put before me and which I accept discloses the following:

(i)

The parents’
relationship is very unstable. Throughout the Society’s involvement the parents
have broken up and reconciled on numerous occasions. The parents have a history
of domestic violence, and have been involved in several incidents of domestic
disputes involving the
Hamilton
Police Services. In February 2000 and
November 2004, the father was charged for assaulting the mother.

(ii)

The family has
been open on an ongoing basis to the Society since
February 4, 2004
, following a domestic dispute between the
mother and father.

(iii)

Throughout the
Society’s involvement, the father has presented as threatening, argumentative,
taunting, intimidating and aggressive towards Society workers and at the children’s
school.

(iv)

The father does
not recognize the impact that domestic abuse has on the children. In June,
2005, the father advised that the domestic violence between him and the mother
has nothing to do with the children.

In
his evidence before me the father did not address the impact of his violence to
the mother in front of the children, other than to say that he lost his temper
and he explained to the children that this was not a good thing.

(v)

To the best of the
Society’s knowledge the parents are currently separated. The mother’s
inconsistency respecting her relationship with the father has been an ongoing
concern. In February 2004, the mother advised that she planned to obtain
custody of the children but by June 2004, the parents were again residing together
in the family home. By September 2004, the parents had another domestic dispute
involving
Hamilton
Police Service and the mother subsequently
completed a custody application. On November 7, 2004, the father gave the
mother a black eye after she allowed him in the family home. In October 2005,
the mother advised the Society that she and the father had once again separated
after trying to make it work for the past three months.

(vi)

The children have
been exposed to the parents’ domestic disputes and have disclosed that they
have witnessed the father hit the mother. Following the domestic incident in
February 2004, the child, M.R.H., disclosed that the parent’s domestic disputes
made her depressed. The child, S.H., disclosed that the mother and father argued
often and it made him feel “a little bit scared”. The child, L.H., disclosed
that he was afraid of people in his family getting hurt and that he was afraid
of getting hurt when his father “cuffs him in the ear”
.

(vii)

The father has
severe, long standing mental health issues for which he currently has refused
treatment or with respect to which the treatment has been unsuccessful. The
father has exhibited concerning behaviour in the presence of the children as
well as Society workers. The Society is not aware of the father receiving any
medical treatment regarding his mental health.

(viii)

In June 2005, the
father denied that he had any mental health concerns.

(ix)

Since the family’s
file opened long term with the Society in February 2004, the mother and father
have moved, both separately and together, approximately 15 times. To the best
of the Society’s knowledge the mother is currently residing in
Newmarket
with relatives and the father is residing in

Hamilton
.

(x)

The father has
made inappropriate comments to the children during supervised access visits.
For example, on
June 22,
2005
, the father advised
the child S.H., that the Society had judged the father as “bad” because of S.H.’s
inappropriate behaviour. In addition the father advised the children that the
visit was being recorded which was not the case. During an access visit in
August 2005, the father told S.H. that a former babysitter had attempted to
murder him.

(xi)

During access
visits, the father has been observed to play roughly with the child S.H.. For
example, during a visit on October 27, 2005, the father grabbed S.H., began
tickling him, pulling his ears and twisting his arm behind his head. When
questioned about this rough play, the father stated that S.H. was strong and
does not know his own strength.

(xii)

Since July 2005,
the mother and father’s access has been placed on hold and reinstated on
several occasions. There have been several concerns respecting the father’s
behaviour with the staff at the Therapeutic Access Centre. On
November 24, 2005
, the father was harassing the Access Centre
receptionist before and after an access visit. After the visit, the father
stood in the doorway and tried to instigate an argument. Two weeks later, on
December 8, 2005, the father became confrontational with the Access Centre Supervisor,
Veronica Phillips, after a mix-up respecting the status of the father’s access
visits. The father stepped in the doorway of Ms. Phillips’ office in a menacing
fashion and asked if she was going to call security.

(xiii)

The father’s
access visits resumed during the week
December 19, 2005
, however, due to the father’s inappropriate
behaviour they are currently supervised at the Society’s office rather than the
Access Centre.

(xiv)

Only the child, S.H.,
currently attends for access visits with the father, as the other children have
advised that they do not want to attend.

(xv)

The mother is
currently residing in
Newmarket
with relatives and has not recently been
attending access visits.

(xvi)

The children are
content in their current placement with their older sibling, N.H..

[
24
]

In giving evidence, Mr.
J.H. failed to specifically address any of the concerns raised by the Society.
The gist of his evidence was that he would be able to adduce evidence at trial
to support the argument that he was not a bad person.

[
25
]

In giving her evidence, Mrs.
W.H. testified that her husband has been facing mental health issues for some
considerable time and that in the year 2000, one of his doctors indicated
“there
was no hope”
. The diagnosis was personality disorder with psychopathic and
sociopathic tendencies.

[
26
]

It was the evidence of Mrs.
W.H. that her husband’s behaviour can at times be unpredictable. He seems to be
fine for periods of time and then his behaviour becomes erratic and tending to
violence toward her. These episodes usually occur when she disagrees with him
or he does not have his way.

[
27
]

The Children’s Lawyer
advises that the two older children, M.R.H., age 14, and L.H., age 11,
confirmed that they have witnessed their father’s violence toward their mother
and have been afraid. They do not wish to return home. S.H., age 9, is more
neutral and tends to downplay the issue of violence.

[
28
]

The only plan of care
filed on behalf of the parents is based upon the parents living together. This
is no longer the case. It was the Society’s evidence that neither parent has
co-operated in the Society’s plan of care.

[
29
]

While there is no
question that it is important that there be due process, where the parents have
had appropriate notice and have failed to respond to the motion fully, have
taken no timely or significant steps as expected in the plan of care and appear
unconvinced that there are any issues that they need to resolve in order to
have their children returned to them, where there is a lot to gain in every
area of expectation and they do not appear to have a realistic plan that can
accommodate the best interests of their children in a long term stable plan,
the motion for summary judgment should succeed.
C.A.S. of Regional Municipality of Waterloo
v. R.S.

2000 CanLII 22902 (ON CJ)
,
[2000] O.J. No.
4880
at para.
28
.

[
30
]

The evidence before me
does not raise triable issues and in my view, the result of a trial is a
foregone conclusion. As a result, summary judgment shall issue in favour of the
Society.

[
31
]

An Order shall issue to
the following effect:

(a)

The children are found to
be non-native, non-Indian and not of the Catholic Faith.

(b)

The children are found to
be in need of protection pursuant to s. 37(2)(b)(i), 37(2)(f), and 37(2)(g) of
the
Child and Family
Services Act
.

(c)

The children, M.R.H.,
date of birth […], 1991; L.H., date of birth […], 1995; and S.H., date of birth
[…], 1997 are made wards of the Society for a period of six months, with access
to the mother and father at the Society’s discretion and supervised in its
discretion.

[
32
]

Supervised access at the
Society’s Offices seems reasonable so far as the father is concerned.

[
33
]

So far as the mother is
concerned, access supervised by her daughter who has custody of the children
appears reasonable provided the daughter is agreeable. Other access in the
Society’s discretion with the approval of the children would appear to be
appropriate.

___________________________

LOFCHIK J.
